title: Deterministic Verification and a Single-Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a sealed, preregistered paired experiment that measured the marginal verifier-detected effect of interposing a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation call per intent reused for both episodes) we generated one candidate per natural-language intent with gpt-5-mini for N = 250 pairs and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate) and guarded (deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if failing, permit one automated repair). Execution completed 500 episodes with model_calls_used = 251. Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The single discordant pair was converted to pass by the single permitted repair. Important scope note: the preregistered sim‑to‑real / production-like confirmatory contrast was not executed; the reported confirmatory estimand applies only to the synthetic/emulation partition executed here. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being explored as intent‑to‑configuration translators in network operations (NetOps), promising faster authoring of device CLI sequences and intent-driven automation. Stochastic generation, however, creates operational risk: syntax errors, incorrect command ordering, local‑policy violations, and vendor‑CLI subtleties can produce unsafe or non‑functional device changes. Prior survey and empirical work documents LLM feasibility for draft configurations while highlighting the continuing need for deterministic verification or human oversight [1], [2].

A common architectural response is to interpose a deterministic validator between generation and acceptance, optionally followed by bounded automated repair — a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pattern — which accepts only validator‑passed candidates or attempts limited repair when mechanically verifiable defects are detected [3], [4]. GVR pipelines reduce mechanically verifiable error classes (syntax, simple ordering and local‑policy violations), but the marginal benefit of such guardrails is unclear when modern LLM outputs already conform to validator encodings under constrained tasks.

Research question. When the same natural‑language intent is realized by an LLM‑generated configuration candidate and checked by a deterministic verifier, how large is the paired difference in verifier‑confirmed intent satisfaction between accepting that candidate unguarded (baseline) and checking it with a deterministic validator plus up to one automated repair (guarded), under shared_initial_candidate semantics? Our contribution is a sealed, preregistered paired experiment (N_pairs = 250) that measures this marginal verifier+single‑repair effect on a synthetic/emulation partition and publishes the full, archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work:
Prior NetOps and LLM literature motivates verifier‑centric pipelines and careful evaluation. NetConfEval and other NetOps studies demonstrate that LLMs can produce usable draft configurations under controlled conditions and that deterministic validators (e.g., Batfish and related header‑space/model‑checking tools) are effective at checking forwarding, reachability, and many local policy properties [1], [3]. Survey articles and recent works on intent‑driven configuration synthesis place generate–verify patterns and program/repair analogs as leading approaches to mitigate mechanical defects in generated code and configurations [2], [4].

Security analyses of prompt injection and indirect injection emphasize the need for filtering and validation layers in LLM‑integrated pipelines but show that adaptive adversaries remain an unresolved threat and that defenses require ongoing evaluation [5]. Our study differs by using a preregistered paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics that isolates the validator/repair marginal effect on identical generated candidates and by archiving deterministic reconciliation and per‑stage accounting so numeric claims are auditable.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered this study as study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1 and froze a confirmatory paired design with N_pairs = 250, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, single permitted automated repair per episode, exclusion/contamination rules, and a primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration SHA‑256 is 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede and is archived with the evidence bundle.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics (precise execution contract). Under shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one initial generation was produced per intent and that same candidate was reused for both the baseline and guarded episodes; no independent first‑pass generations per condition were produced. Provider audit reconciles to hosted_model_call_event_count = 251 and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}, i.e., 250 shared initial generations plus a single repair call (deterministic reconciliation artifact archived).

Task generation, constraints and validators. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 250 constrained intent tasks. Each task encoded initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and workflow policies (make‑before‑break, group minima, protected interfaces) to exercise ordering and local‑policy constraints. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing full_intent_constraint_validation (syntax parsing, required_sequence ordering checks, final_state snapshot comparison). Validator outputs include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, violation_codes, and boolean valid. When valid = false and the episode was in the guarded arm the pipeline permitted up to one deterministic template repair (reordering, splitting/joining CLI lines, simple token ordering fixes) after which the validator was re‑applied. No multi‑iteration free‑form repair or human escalation was allowed.

Inclusion/exclusion, contamination, and missingness. Exclusion rules removed items that failed vendor parser deterministically, or that matched denylist hashes or credential‑like tokens. Contamination detectors flagged instruction‑like embedded tokens; flagged items were to be excluded from primary analysis. In the executed confirmatory partition no episodes were excluded or flagged and complete_pair_count = 250.

Statistical analysis. The preregistered primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1: an exact two‑sided McNemar test on paired binaries and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) for guarded − baseline difference. Sensitivity analyses (per preregistration) treat incomplete pairs conservatively as failures; no such treatment was required because there were no incomplete pairs.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and raw counts. Execution completed the confirmatory partition with planned_episode_count = 500, completed_episode_count = 500, complete_pair_count = 250, and model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair). The single repair call is reflected in adapter stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}.

Primary outcomes and contingency. Validator‑scored successes: baseline_success_count = 249 (baseline_success_rate = 0.996), guarded_success_count = 250 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The lone discordant pair corresponds to the sole exercised repair; repair conversion rate on the confirmatory partition = 1/250 = 0.4%.

Statistical inference. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 on discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0). Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for guarded − baseline (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.012] (0.0 – 1.2 percentage points). These numeric outputs are recorded in the archived analysis artifacts.

Representative validator diagnostics. Passed episodes show parsed_command_count equal to required_command_count as encoded by the task payloads. Representative artifacts (e.g., task‑000003) show parsed_command_count = required_command_count = 6 and valid = true for both baseline and guarded episodes. No contamination flags or verifier runtime errors occurred in the confirmatory partition.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and operational meaning. Under the constrained synthetic/emulation tasks executed here and the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, the marginal verifier‑detected benefit of inserting a deterministic validator plus one permitted repair was small: initial gpt‑5‑mini candidates satisfied the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases and the single exercised repair converted the only failing candidate. The paired‑bootstrap CI upper bound (1.2 pp) supplies an empirical bound on plausible verifier‑detected improvement under these conditions.

Factors explaining the small observed gain. Artifact‑grounded causes include: (1) the deterministic task generator produced constrained intents with explicit allowed_touched_fields and required_sequences that reduce task ambiguity and encourage well‑formed CLI outputs; (2) the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) produced highly consistent, syntactically well‑formed sequences for these constrained tasks; and (3) the deterministic validator only checks mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, ordering, final_state snapshot) and does not assess live protocol dynamics or emergent cross‑device behavior.

Power and preregistration assumptions. The preregistration power calculation assumed a baseline pass rate ≈ 0.90 to detect a 15 pp effect with ≈80% power and selected N_pairs = 250 accordingly. The realized baseline pass rate (0.996) was substantially higher than assumed; this reduces the ability to detect small absolute improvements and makes the bootstrap CI the most informative result for bounding likely effects.

Threats to validity. Internal validity depends on prompt templates, the single‑repair policy, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. Construct validity is limited because the validator measures mechanical correctness rather than protocol‑level behavioral correctness. External validity is limited to the synthetic/emulation partition executed here; preregistered community and production‑like partitions were not executed. Security analyses (adaptive prompt‑injection, retrieval attacks) were not exercised and remain open threats.

Reproducibility and auditability. Key reconciliation facts reported above (model_calls_used = 251, stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}, contingency counts n11 = 249 / n10 = 1 / n01 = 0 / n00 = 0) are directly reproducible from the archived execution manifest and analysis CSVs. The evidence bundle contains the full execution and analysis manifests and per‑artifact hashes; a concise pointer to that manifest is provided in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the verifier‑detected marginal benefit of deterministic validation plus one permitted automated repair on identical LLM‑generated configuration candidates. In N = 250 constrained synthetic intent tasks, initial gpt‑5‑mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases; the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate via the single permitted repair. Observed paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp]; p = 1.0). We explicitly disclose that the preregistered sim‑to‑real confirmatory contrast was not executed; the executed confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on the synthetic/emulation partition only. Broader production, adversarial, multi‑model, and multi‑iteration repair evaluations remain necessary to establish generality. All execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts referenced in this paper are archived in the evidence bundle described in the Disclosure Statement.

disclosure_statement:
Human role and autonomy boundary: Following the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track autonomy lock, the autonomous system performed literature search, study selection, preregistration freeze, prompt preservation, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, autonomous peer review and revision, and finalization without manual human editing of technical content. A human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and conducted pre‑lock infrastructure development; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.

Models, tools, and manifest pointer: Declared model used for initial generations = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). Deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The archived evidence bundle contains the full execution and analysis manifests and per‑artifact hashes; a single concise manifest pointer is provided for audit: execution/execution_manifest.json (this manifest contains the full artifact-level hashes and paths required to reconstruct execution and analysis). Preregistration SHA‑256 (immutable): 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede.

Initial master prompt (immutable reference): provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba.

Preregistered contract and executed estimand: The study was preregistered to run a confirmatory paired design with generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, permitted up to one automated repair per episode, and primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Deviation disclosure: the preregistered sim‑to‑real / production‑like confirmatory contrast was not executed; the executed confirmatory estimand and reported inferential statistics apply only to the synthetic/emulation partition (N_pairs = 250) described in the preregistration and archived manifests.

Auditable numeric reconciliation facts (concise): planned_episode_count = 500, completed_episode_count = 500, complete_pair_count = 250, model_calls_used = 251, stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}, contingency counts n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Full reconstruction is possible from execution/execution_manifest.json and the preregistration and master prompt artifacts listed above.
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production‑like partitions were not executed and remain exploratory.

Deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences) but did not measure broader semantic or behavioral correctness (protocol dynamics, emergent interactions).
Only one declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi‑model or alternate‑validator generality.
Only a single automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi‑iteration repairs or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation were not evaluated.
Adversarial and retrieval‑based attacks (adaptive prompt‑injection, vendor‑targeted exploit vectors) and large‑scale production heterogeneity were not exercised and remain open threats.
